6540: When used as a verb, "fox" draws directly from the image of a fox as an animal — sly, clever, and hard to catch. So whenever you see "fox" used as an action word, think of that craftiness. It almost always carries the sense of cunning, confusion, or deception.

1. To Trick or Deceive Someone (Most Common)

This is the most widely used meaning. To fox someone means to cleverly fool or outwit them — not by force, but by being smart and sneaky about it.

"The magician foxed the entire audience with his trick."
"She foxed her competitors by pretending to be weaker than she was."

The key idea here is intentional deception. The person doing the foxing is being deliberately cunning. It's not just a simple lie — it's a smart, strategic move that leaves the other person completely caught off guard.

2. To Baffle or Confuse Someone

This is closely related to the first meaning but has a slightly different flavor. Here, fox means to completely puzzle or bewilder someone — to leave them scratching their head.

"This question has foxed scientists for decades."
"I've read the instructions three times, but they still fox me."

Notice the difference: in meaning #1, someone is being deliberately tricked by another person. In this meaning, the "foxing" can happen without any intention — a difficult problem, a strange situation, or confusing information can fox you. You are simply left confused and unable to figure something out.

This meaning is especially common in British English, and it is very natural in everyday speech.

3. To Make Someone Appear Confused or Foolish (by Outsmarting Them)

This is an extension of the first meaning, but it emphasizes the result — that the person being foxed ends up looking foolish because they were outmaneuvered.

"The defendant foxed the lawyer with an answer nobody expected."

You will very often see "fox" used in the passive voice, meaning something was done to a person — they were the one confused or tricked, not the one doing it.

"I was completely foxed by her explanation."
"He looked foxed when she changed her story."
"We were foxed into signing the wrong document."

"Foxed" is actually one of the most natural ways this verb appears in real usage, so it's important to get comfortable with it.
A Completely Separate Meaning: When Paper or Books Are "Foxed"

This is a very specific use of the word, unrelated to trickery or confusion. When old books, documents, or paper develop brownish or yellowish spots due to age, moisture, or mold, they are described as being foxed.

"The pages of the antique Bible were badly foxed."
"The print had foxed around the edges after years in storage."

You would only encounter this meaning in the context of antiques, rare books, old documents, or art restoration. It simply means the paper has deteriorated and become discolored with age-related spotting.

In older, mostly archaic English, "to fox" someone could mean to make them drunk. You are unlikely to encounter this in modern writing or speech, but you may come across it in older literature.

"He was foxed by the evening's ale." (old-fashioned)
Putting It All Together: What Kind of Word Is It?

"Fox" as a verb is:

  • Informal to semi-formal in tone. It sounds natural in both casual conversation and in newspapers or non-fiction writing.
  • More common in British English than American English, particularly the "baffle/confuse" sense. Americans more commonly use words like "trick," "fool," or "baffle" instead, but "fox" is perfectly understood everywhere.
  • Vivid and expressive. Choosing "foxed" instead of "confused" or "tricked" adds a touch of color and sharpness to your language. It implies cleverness was involved — either someone cleverly deceived you, or the problem was so clever it beat you.

• To fox someone = to trick or deceive them cleverly
  • To fox someone = to completely baffle or confuse them
  • To be foxed = to be left confused or outsmarted (passive; very common)
  • Paper/books are foxed = they have developed brown spots from age (specific, technical context)
  • To fox someone (archaic) = to make them drunk (rarely used today)

The heart of this word, in almost every case, is cleverness meeting confusion — either someone is being smart enough to fool you, or something is too complex for you to figure out.
6541:
A foxhole is a small hole dug into the ground by a soldier during a battle or war, used as a hiding place and protection from enemy fire.

That's the heart of it. Now let's build a complete picture.

Imagine a soldier on a battlefield. Bullets are flying. Bombs are falling. There's no wall, no building, no barrier nearby. What does the soldier do? He grabs a shovel and starts digging — fast — right into the ground beneath his feet.

The hole he digs is called a foxhole.

It's roughly the shape and size of a bathtub, or sometimes even smaller — just large enough for one or two people to crouch or lie down in. It's typically about chest-deep when you're standing, so a soldier inside it has their upper body below ground level, shielded from bullets and shrapnel (the flying metal fragments from exploding bombs). The soldier can still peek over the edge to watch for the enemy or fire a weapon, but most of their body is protected by the surrounding earth.

It is dug quickly, under pressure, with basic tools — sometimes just a small folding shovel called an entrenching tool. It is not meant to be permanent or comfortable. It's a survival measure.

The word combines "fox" and "hole." Foxes are known for digging burrows and hiding in the ground to escape danger. A soldier in combat does something very similar — they dig into the ground and take cover, just like a cornered fox would. The comparison is vivid and fitting.

• "The soldiers dug foxholes before nightfall so they'd be protected when the enemy attacked at dawn."
  • "He spent three freezing nights in a muddy foxhole, waiting for orders to advance."
  • "The sergeant ordered his men to take cover in their foxholes as the artillery shells began to fall."
The Difference Between a Foxhole, a Trench, and a Bunker

Since these three words all involve soldiers hiding underground or in covered spaces, it helps to know how they differ:

  • A foxhole is small, hastily dug, and meant for one or two people. It's a temporary, quick solution made in the heat of battle.
  • A trench is a long, narrow ditch dug in a line, meant for many soldiers to take cover together and move along. Trenches are more organized and longer-lasting (famously used in World War I).
  • A bunker is a reinforced, fortified underground shelter — built with concrete or thick materials to withstand heavy bombardment. It's stronger and more permanent than either a foxhole or a trench.

So a foxhole is the most basic and improvised of the three.

Outside of literal warfare, people also use foxhole figuratively to mean any place of safety or retreat when things get very difficult or dangerous — not just in a physical sense, but also emotionally or professionally.

For example:

  • "When the media criticism became unbearable, the politician retreated to his foxhole and stopped giving interviews."

Here, "foxhole" means a personal safe space — a place to hide and wait until the pressure dies down. The idea is the same: danger surrounds you, so you take cover.
A Famous Expression: "There Are No Atheists in Foxholes"

This is a very well-known English saying, and understanding it will help you deeply understand the cultural weight the word carries.

The expression means: when people are in extreme danger and face the real possibility of death, even those who don't normally believe in God tend to pray or turn to religion for comfort.

The idea is that a foxhole — where a soldier is under fire and might die at any moment — is a place of such raw fear and desperation that it strips away all pretense. In that moment, no one is too proud or too rational to pray.

This phrase is widely quoted and debated. It shows how deeply the word "foxhole" is associated in English with a life-or-death situation and with being pushed to one's absolute limits.

Sometimes people use the expression "foxhole buddy" or "foxhole friend" to describe someone you trust completely — someone you would literally be willing to be in a dangerous situation with, side by side. It's a way of saying: "This is someone I trust with my life."

It's used informally in everyday speech, not just in military contexts:

  • "She's my foxhole buddy — I'd trust her with anything."
Summary: What You Need to Remember

AspectDetail
Literal meaningA small pit dug by soldiers in the ground for protection from enemy fire
SizeJust big enough for 1–2 people to crouch or lie in
PurposeImmediate protection during combat — shields the body using the earth itself
Figurative meaningAny personal retreat or safe space during a difficult time
Cultural weightRepresents extreme danger, survival, and being pushed to one's limits

The word "foxhole" is compact but carries enormous weight. It speaks to human vulnerability, survival instinct, and the desperate ingenuity of people under fire — whether on a battlefield or in life.
6542:
A foyer is the first room or area you enter when you walk into a building — the space that sits right at the entrance, between the outside world and the rest of the interior.

Think of it as a "transition zone." When you open the front door of a place, you don't always walk straight into the living room or the main hall. Often, there's a small space in between — that's the foyer.

Foyers appear in two main kinds of places:

1. In homes and apartments
When you enter someone's house, there's often a small area near the front door — sometimes with a coat rack, a mirror, a small table, or a shoe rack. That space is the foyer. It's where guests are greeted and where you prepare to move deeper into the home. In modest homes, it might just be a narrow hallway. In larger or more elegant homes, it can be quite spacious and decorated to make a strong first impression.

2. In public buildings — especially hotels, theaters, and opera houses
This is where the word is used most grandly. When you walk into a fancy hotel, you first enter a large, often beautifully decorated space before you reach the reception desk or the elevators. That's the foyer (though it's also commonly called a lobby in this context).

In theaters and cinemas, the foyer is the open area inside the entrance where people gather before the show begins or during the interval (intermission). It's where you might buy a ticket, collect your program, or simply wait and mingle. It serves as a gathering and social space.

A foyer serves several practical and social functions:

  • It acts as a buffer between the noise, weather, and chaos of the outside, and the calmer interior of the building.
  • It signals entry. It tells you: you've arrived, but you haven't fully entered yet. It's a moment of transition.
  • It receives guests. Hosts often greet visitors in the foyer before leading them further inside.
  • It provides a place to pause and prepare — to take off your coat, leave your umbrella, check your appearance in a mirror, or simply orient yourself.
  • In public venues, it creates a social gathering space before or after the main event.

A foyer can be:

  • Small and functional — just enough space for a door, a mat, and a hook for coats (common in apartments or modest homes).
  • Medium-sized and welcoming — with some furniture like a console table, a lamp, artwork, and a mirror (common in larger homes).
  • Grand and impressive — high ceilings, marble floors, chandeliers, sweeping staircases (common in luxury hotels, theaters, mansions, and government buildings).

The size and décor of a foyer often reflect the character or status of the building it belongs to. A grand foyer in a five-star hotel is designed to awe you the moment you walk in. A simple foyer in a small home is designed simply to welcome you.

You'll often encounter words used alongside or instead of "foyer." Here's how they relate:

  • Lobby — Almost identical in meaning. Used more commonly for public buildings (hotels, offices, apartment buildings). A lobby tends to be larger and more functional (with a reception desk, seating area, etc.). Foyer carries a slightly more elegant or theatrical feel.
  • Entrance hall — A very straightforward term; essentially the same idea. Used more in everyday British English for the space just inside the front door of a home.
  • Vestibule — A small enclosed space right at the entry of a building, often with two sets of doors (one to the outside, one to the interior). It's more specific and architectural — it acts as an airlock of sorts, keeping cold air out. Smaller and more functional than a foyer.
  • Anteroom — A room that leads into a larger, more important room. Similar transitional purpose, but more often used for formal or official settings (e.g., an anteroom outside a courtroom or a royal chamber).

So while all these words describe transitional entry spaces, foyer sits in the middle — more elegant than "entrance hall," more graceful than "vestibule," and slightly more intimate or aesthetic than "lobby."

Here are natural examples of how the word is used:

  • "Please wait in the foyer — I'll let them know you've arrived."
  • "The hotel's foyer had a grand chandelier and marble floors."
  • "She hung her coat in the foyer before coming into the living room."
  • "During the interval, the audience gathered in the theater's foyer for drinks."
  • "The apartment was small, but the foyer gave it a welcoming feel."
A foyer is the entrance area of a building — the transitional space between the outside and the interior — where guests are received, coats are left, and first impressions are made.
6543: "Frabjous" means wonderfully joyous and delightful — describing something so good, so exciting, and so celebratory that it fills you with a feeling of pure, triumphant happiness. It's not ordinary, quiet contentment. It's beaming, arms-in-the-air, heart-bursting joy mixed with a sense of triumph.

Think about the difference between feeling "happy" and feeling ecstatic. Frabjous lives in the ecstatic zone — but it adds something extra: a playful, almost magical quality to the joy.

Imagine you've just heard the best news of your life, or a long-awaited victory finally arrived. That specific feeling — giddy, triumphant, wonderful, almost unreal — is exactly what frabjous describes.

As an adjective, it most naturally describes moments, days, events, and occasions — not physical objects. You would say:

  • "What a frabjous day this has been!"
  • "It was a truly frabjous moment when they called my name."
  • "The celebration was completely frabjous."
  • "She was in a frabjous mood all afternoon."

You wouldn't naturally call a chair or a sandwich frabjous. The word belongs to the world of feelings, experiences, and events.
Where it comes from (context, not etymology)

The word was invented by the poet Lewis Carroll in his famous nonsense poem Jabberwocky (from Through the Looking-Glass, 1871). The key line is:

"O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!"

A father is bursting with celebration because his son has slain the fearsome Jabberwock. That context tells you everything about the word's emotional weight: it's the word you reach for when a moment is so magnificent, so triumphant, and so wonderful that ordinary words simply aren't enough.

Even though Carroll invented it for a whimsical poem, the word has since been recognized in real dictionaries (including Merriam-Webster), making it a legitimate English adjective.
How it differs from similar words

• Happy — mild, everyday. Frabjous is far more intense and exuberant.
  • Joyful — warm and sincere, but quiet. Frabjous is louder, more triumphant.
  • Wonderful — very good. Frabjous is so wonderful it almost makes you want to shout.
  • Glorious — grand and majestic, but stiff. Frabjous is grand and playfully light-hearted.
  • Fantastic/Fabulous — strong positives, but casual and common. Frabjous is rarer and carries a literary, imaginative flair.

The key thing that sets frabjous apart from all of these is its combination of joy + triumph + whimsy, all in one word.

Frabjous is informal and literary. You would never write it in a business email, a legal document, or a scientific paper. It belongs in:

  • Casual conversation when you want to sound expressive, witty, or clever
  • Creative or playful writing
  • Any moment where you want a single word that radiates jubilant, celebratory delight

When you use it in conversation, people may smile — it's an unusual, charming word, and using it signals that you are both well-read and have a playful spirit.

Frabjous describes something so wonderfully joyous, triumphant, and delightful that it fills you with a feeling of giddy, almost magical happiness — the kind of happiness that ordinary words struggle to contain.
6544:
A fracas is a noisy, chaotic, disorderly disturbance — usually a quarrel or a minor fight — that happens suddenly and involves a messy mix of shouting, confusion, and sometimes physical scuffling. Think of it as a scene that erupts — loud, unruly, and hard to ignore.

The single most important thing to understand about a fracas is this: it is defined by two things happening together — noise AND disorder. Take away either one, and it stops being a fracas.
Breaking It Down: What Makes Something a Fracas

A fracas has several defining qualities, and understanding each one will sharpen your feel for the word.

It is noisy. A fracas is never quiet. There is shouting, yelling, possibly crashing or clattering. If people are having a heated disagreement in hushed, controlled tones, that is not a fracas. The noise is almost always part of what makes it noticeable to others nearby.

It is disorderly and chaotic. A fracas is messy and confused. Nobody is in control. Things are happening all at once — people talking over each other, possibly pushing or shoving, bystanders getting drawn in. There is no structure or clear progression.

It involves conflict. A fracas is not just general noise — it centers around a dispute, argument, or minor physical altercation. There is tension and friction between the people involved. It is not a party getting loud; it is a confrontation getting out of hand.

It is usually brief and spontaneous. A fracas tends to flare up quickly and burn out relatively fast. It is not a prolonged, organized conflict. It erupts, creates chaos, and eventually dies down.

It usually involves multiple people, or at least creates a public scene. While two people can technically be involved, a fracas often implies that others are caught up in it — whether as participants, witnesses, or people being disrupted by it.

This is an important nuance. A fracas sits in the middle of the severity scale — it is more than a simple argument, but less than a serious violent fight or riot.

It is serious enough to cause a visible disturbance and draw attention, but not so serious that people are gravely hurt or that it constitutes an organized assault. It is the kind of thing that might get reported to security, make a small news item, or get people ejected from a venue — but it is not a war, a riot, or a brutal attack.
Fracas vs. Similar Words (So You Never Confuse Them)

Fracas vs. Quarrel: A quarrel is a verbal disagreement, which can be quiet and private. A fracas is loud and public, and often goes beyond just words.

Fracas vs. Brawl: A brawl is a more intense, primarily physical fight. A fracas has a stronger emphasis on noise and confusion, and may not be very physical at all — it could be mostly shouting and chaos.

Fracas vs. Commotion: A commotion is general noise and disorder, but does not necessarily involve conflict. A fracas always has some element of dispute or confrontation at its center.

Fracas vs. Melee: A melee specifically describes a confused, large-scale physical fight involving many people. A fracas is broader — it can be mostly verbal, and can involve fewer people.
Where You Will See This Word Used

Fracas is commonly used in:

News and journalism — reporters use it to describe minor but dramatic public disturbances. For example: "A fracas broke out in the stands after the referee's controversial decision."

Political and social contexts — to describe heated, disorderly confrontations between groups, without calling them full-on fights. For example: "A fracas erupted outside the council meeting as protesters clashed with supporters."

Everyday storytelling — when someone is recounting a chaotic, dramatic incident. For example: "I wanted a quiet evening, but somehow ended up in the middle of a fracas at the restaurant."
Example Sentences to Cement Your Understanding

• The birthday party turned into a fracas when two guests got into a heated argument over the music.
  • Police were called to break up the fracas that had spilled out of the bar and into the street.
  • What started as a minor disagreement quickly turned into a full-blown fracas, with half the team shouting at once.
  • She tried to stay calm but got caught up in the fracas before she even understood what it was about.
  • The fracas lasted only a few minutes, but it left the whole lobby in disarray.

If you want one clear image to hold in your mind: imagine a scene that is loud, messy, and out of control — people in conflict, voices raised, things chaotic — a situation that has slipped past the point of calm argument but has not yet become a full-scale violent fight. That is a fracas. It is the word for when a disagreement goes public, gets noisy, and loses all sense of order.
6545: Fracking is a method of drilling deep into the Earth to extract oil and natural gas that are trapped inside hard rock formations underground.

Deep beneath the ground, there are layers of rock — sometimes a type called shale — that contain oil and natural gas locked inside tiny pores and cracks within the rock. Think of it like oil and gas trapped inside a very dense sponge made of stone. Traditional drilling methods couldn't get this fuel out efficiently, because the rock is too tight and compact for the oil or gas to flow freely to the surface on its own.

Fracking solves this problem by breaking the rock open from the inside to release what's trapped within it.

Here's the process in plain terms:

  1. A deep hole is drilled into the ground — often several kilometres deep — until it reaches the rock layer containing oil or gas. Modern fracking wells are often drilled vertically first, and then horizontally through the rock layer to reach more of it.
  2. A high-pressure mixture is pumped down into the well. This mixture is mostly water (enormous quantities of it), combined with sand and a small amount of chemical additives. This fluid is injected at such extreme pressure that it literally cracks or fractures the surrounding rock.
  3. The cracks spread outward through the rock in multiple directions, opening up pathways that didn't exist before.
  4. The sand in the mixture plays a clever role: it gets lodged inside these newly created cracks and holds them open, like tiny wedges, so the cracks don't close back up once the pressure is released.
  5. Oil and natural gas, now freed from the fractured rock, flow through these open cracks into the well, and are then pumped up to the surface.
  6. The water used in the process largely comes back up as well, now mixed with various underground substances. This returned water — called flowback water or produced water — must be treated or disposed of carefully.

The word "fracking" itself is simply a shortening of hydraulic fracturing — "hydraulic" meaning it uses liquid under pressure, and "fracturing" meaning the deliberate cracking of rock.
Why It Became Such a Big Deal

Before fracking was developed and widely used (it gained enormous momentum in the early 2000s, particularly in the United States), vast reservoirs of oil and gas locked in shale rock were considered economically unworkable — the fuel was known to be there, but there was no practical way to extract it profitably.

Fracking changed this completely. It unlocked previously inaccessible reserves and triggered what is often called the "shale revolution" or "shale boom" — a dramatic surge in oil and gas production, especially in the United States, which went on to become the world's largest producer of both oil and natural gas. Countries like Canada, Australia, Argentina, and China also have significant fracking operations.

This had wide-ranging effects: it lowered energy prices in certain markets, reduced some countries' dependence on imported oil, created large numbers of jobs, and shifted global geopolitics around energy.

Fracking is one of the most debated industrial practices in the world. While it has economic advantages, it also carries a range of serious concerns:

1. Water contamination
One of the biggest fears is that the chemical-laced fracking fluid, or the oil and gas released underground, can leak into nearby groundwater supplies — the underground water that many communities rely on for drinking. While the industry argues that properly constructed wells prevent this, there have been documented cases of contamination, and the risk remains a central point of debate.

2. Enormous water usage
A single fracking well can use millions of litres of water. In regions already facing water scarcity, this creates direct competition with agricultural, residential, and ecological water needs.

3. Wastewater disposal and earthquakes
The large volumes of wastewater produced by fracking are often injected deep underground for disposal. This has been strongly linked to a measurable increase in induced seismicity — that is, earthquakes triggered by human activity. Several regions in the United States that previously had almost no seismic activity have experienced thousands of small to moderate earthquakes after large-scale fracking and wastewater injection operations began.

4. Methane leaks
Natural gas is mostly methane, which is a very potent greenhouse gas — far more powerful than carbon dioxide in trapping heat in the atmosphere over the short term. During fracking operations, methane can leak into the air from wells, pipelines, and equipment. These leaks, called fugitive emissions, partly undermine the argument that natural gas is a cleaner alternative to coal.

5. Air pollution
Fracking sites release various air pollutants beyond methane, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and other chemicals, which can contribute to smog and respiratory health problems in nearby communities.

6. Landscape and community disruption
Fracking operations involve heavy industrial infrastructure — drilling rigs, storage tanks, pipelines, heavy truck traffic, noise, and lights. This can disrupt ecosystems, fragment wildlife habitats, and significantly affect the quality of life for people living near these sites.

7. Climate implications
Because fracking makes fossil fuels cheaper and more abundant to extract, critics argue it extends society's dependence on oil and gas at a time when the world urgently needs to shift toward renewable energy to address climate change. Supporters counter that natural gas, when it burns, produces fewer carbon emissions than coal, making it a useful "transition fuel."

Because of these environmental concerns, fracking has been banned or placed under moratoriums in several countries and regions — including France, Germany, Ireland, Scotland, and certain states and provinces in North America. Other governments actively support it as a pillar of energy security and economic development. It sits at the centre of ongoing debates about energy policy, climate responsibility, environmental protection, and economic interests.

Fracking is the industrial process of blasting water, sand, and chemicals at high pressure into underground rock to crack it open and release the oil and natural gas trapped within. It has dramatically expanded the world's accessible fossil fuel supplies but has also raised serious, well-documented concerns about water safety, air quality, earthquakes, methane emissions, and its broader role in the climate crisis. It represents one of the defining tensions of our era: short-term economic and energy benefits weighed against long-term environmental consequences.
6546: A fraction is a way of expressing a part of a whole, or more precisely, a division of one quantity by another. The word "fraction" has two main lives — one in mathematics (its primary and most detailed meaning), and one in everyday general language.

What It Looks Like

A fraction is written as one number placed above another number, with a horizontal line between them:

3/4 — here, 3 is on top, 4 is on the bottom.

The top number is called the numerator, and the bottom number is called the denominator.

What the Two Numbers Mean

  • The denominator (bottom) tells you into how many equal parts the whole thing has been divided.
  • The numerator (top) tells you how many of those parts you are talking about.

Example: Imagine a pizza cut into 4 equal slices. If you take 3 slices, you have 3/4 (three-fourths) of the pizza. The pizza was divided into 4 parts (denominator = 4), and you have 3 of them (numerator = 3).

A Fraction Is Also a Division

A fraction is simply a way of writing a division problem. 3/4 means exactly the same thing as 3 ÷ 4. When you do that division, you get 0.75. So a fraction and its decimal form are two ways of writing the same value.

This is important: fractions are not just "parts of a pizza." They are numbers — they have their own place on the number line, just like whole numbers do.

Proper Fraction

The numerator is smaller than the denominator. The value of the fraction is less than 1 (less than a whole).

Examples: 1/2, 3/4, 5/8, 2/7

These represent "less than one whole thing."

Improper Fraction

The numerator is equal to or larger than the denominator. The value is 1 or more.

Examples: 4/4, 7/3, 11/5

4/4 means all 4 slices of a 4-slice pizza — that's the whole pizza, equal to 1. 7/3 means 7 parts when the whole was divided into 3, which is more than one whole — it equals about 2.33.

Mixed Number

A mixed number is a whole number written alongside a proper fraction, like 2½ or 3¾. It is another way of expressing an improper fraction. For example, 7/3 = 2⅓ (two whole ones and one-third more). Mixed numbers and improper fractions represent the same values, just written differently.

Unit Fraction

A fraction with 1 as the numerator: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/100. These represent exactly one part of a divided whole. They are the building blocks of all other fractions — for example, 3/4 is simply three copies of 1/4.

Equivalent Fractions

Different fractions that represent the exact same value are called equivalent fractions.

1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 50/100 — all of these are the same amount.

Think of it this way: whether you cut a chocolate bar into 2 pieces and take 1, or cut it into 4 pieces and take 2, you have the same amount of chocolate.

You create equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing both the numerator and denominator by the same number.

Simplified (Reduced) Fraction

A fraction is in its simplest form (also called reduced form) when the numerator and denominator share no common divisor other than 1. For example, 4/8 can be simplified to 1/2 by dividing both by 4. The simplest form of a fraction is generally preferred for clarity.
Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages — The Same Idea, Three Different Outfits

Fractions, decimals, and percentages are three different ways of expressing the same concept: a part of a whole.

  • 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%
  • 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%
  • 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%

A decimal fraction is any number with a decimal point — like 0.3 or 0.75 — and it is a fraction expressed in powers of 10 (0.3 = 3/10, 0.75 = 75/100). So all decimals are technically fractions.

Adding and Subtracting

You can only directly add or subtract fractions that have the same denominator (called a common denominator).

  • 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4 — easy, same denominator.
  • 1/3 + 1/4 — different denominators, so you first convert them to a common denominator (1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12), then add: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

Multiplying

Multiply numerator by numerator, and denominator by denominator.

  • 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2

Dividing

Flip the second fraction (swap its numerator and denominator — this is called the reciprocal), then multiply.

  • 2/3 ÷ 1/4 = 2/3 × 4/1 = 8/3

Fractions fill in all the gaps between whole numbers on the number line. Between 0 and 1, you have 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, and infinitely many others. Between 1 and 2, you have 1¼, 1½, 1¾, and so on. This is part of why fractions are fundamental to mathematics — they allow us to measure and express values with precision that whole numbers alone cannot.

Outside of mathematics, "fraction" is commonly used to simply mean a small part or portion of something — not necessarily mathematically precise.

  • "Only a fraction of the audience stayed until the end." — a small part of the audience.
  • "You can buy it online for a fraction of the price." — for much less money.
  • "She moved just a fraction to the left." — a tiny amount.

In this everyday sense, "fraction" conveys smallness and incompleteness. When someone says something costs "a fraction of what it used to," they mean it is much cheaper now — a small part of the original price.

Note the nuance: in math, a fraction can be greater than 1 (like 7/3), but in everyday language, saying "a fraction of something" almost always implies something small.

In chemistry and related sciences, a fraction refers to a component separated from a mixture during a process called fractional distillation. For example, crude oil is heated and its different components (such as petrol, diesel, kerosene) separate out at different temperatures — each separated component is called a fraction. Here the word carries the same spirit: a part separated from a whole mixture.

• "A fraction of the cost/time/price" — much cheaper, faster, or smaller than expected.
  • "In a fraction of a second" — an extremely short moment, less than a full second.
  • "A small/tiny fraction" — emphasizes how little the portion is.
  • "By a fraction" — by a very small margin (e.g., "She missed the record by a fraction").

Fraction (noun) means a part of something divided into equal portions, expressed as one number over another. In mathematics, it is a precise numerical concept representing division. In everyday language, it loosely means a small portion of something. In science, it refers to a separated component of a mixture. The thread connecting all three uses is the same: a piece, not the whole.
6547: Fractious describes something — or someone — that is irritable, quarrelsome, and difficult to manage or control. Think of it as two qualities bundled into one word: being easy to upset or annoy, and being actively hard to deal with as a result of that irritability.
When it describes a person or animal

When fractious is used for a person or an animal, it means they are in a bad, fussy, or peevish state and are resisting all attempts to be calmed or controlled. A fractious baby cries, fusses, and refuses to settle no matter what you try. A fractious horse won't cooperate with its rider and keeps acting up. A fractious patient at a hospital snaps at nurses and refuses to follow instructions.

Notice that fractious goes beyond just being "grumpy." A grumpy person might sit quietly in a corner with a scowl — passive and unpleasant but not causing real trouble. A fractious person is actively difficult: resisting, pushing back, snapping, throwing things off course, and making life hard for whoever is trying to manage them. The grumpiness has teeth.
When it describes a group, situation, or relationship

This is where fractious really earns its place. It is very commonly used to describe groups of people, organizations, debates, negotiations, alliances, or relationships. In this sense, it means something full of internal conflict and disagreement — hard to hold together and hard to move forward.

A fractious political party is one where members constantly fight among themselves, block each other, and can never agree. A fractious negotiation is one where every point is disputed and the talks keep breaking down. A fractious coalition is an alliance where the members distrust each other and pull in opposite directions. A fractious debate is one where the participants keep clashing, interrupting, and inflaming each other instead of making progress.

The core idea is exactly the same as when it's used for a person — difficulty, resistance, conflict — but now applied to groups and situations rather than a single individual.
How it compares to similar words

Knowing how fractious differs from nearby words is one of the best ways to pin down its exact meaning.

Irritable simply means someone is easily annoyed or upset. Fractious goes further — not only are they irritable, they are actively difficult to deal with because of it. Irritable is the cause; fractious is the full picture.

Grumpy or cranky describe a bad mood, but in a quiet, mostly passive way. A fractious person is louder and harder to manage — the bad mood spills outward and creates real disruption.

Unruly means hard to control, but it doesn't necessarily involve irritability or a bad temper. A fractious thing is hard to control specifically because of its quarrelsome, emotionally charged quality. Unruly is about behavior; fractious is about behavior driven by a combative spirit.

Quarrelsome describes a person who likes to argue and pick fights. Fractious includes this quality but is broader — it applies to moods, organizations, whole political situations, and group dynamics, not just a person's habit of picking fights.
Real sentences to see it in action

"The fractious toddler refused to eat, sleep, or be comforted for hours." (irritable and hard to manage)

"The committee meeting turned fractious, with members interrupting each other and storming out." (full of conflict, hard to control)

"Managing the fractious coalition required enormous diplomatic skill." (an alliance riven by internal disagreements)

"The normally calm horse became fractious during the thunderstorm." (agitated, uncooperative, difficult to handle)

"The country's fractious politics made it nearly impossible to pass any legislation." (a political environment defined by conflict and division)
The register and feel of this word

Fractious is a formal-leaning word. You are far more likely to encounter it in a newspaper, a novel, or an essay than in casual everyday speech. In conversation, people tend to reach for "difficult," "cranky," "touchy," or "contentious" instead. So when you spot fractious, it's almost always in something written, and it signals a slightly elevated, precise use of language.

Whenever you see this word, ask yourself: Is this thing irritable, conflict-prone, and hard to manage? If yes — whether it's a child, a horse, a parliament, a marriage, or a negotiation — fractious is doing its job perfectly.
6548:
To fracture something means to break or crack it — but not just anything. Fracturing specifically happens to things that are hard, rigid, and solid, like bones, rocks, glass, ice, or concrete. When something fractures, a force acts on it powerfully enough to split or crack its inner structure.

The most important thing to understand right away is this: fracturing does not always mean something breaks into separate pieces. A fractured bone can still look like a whole bone from the outside — the damage is internal, in the form of a crack running through it. This is what makes "fracture" its own precise word, different from words like "shatter" or "crumble."

Think of a bone in your arm. It is hard and dense. If you fall and land badly, the force of the impact can be powerful enough to crack the bone from inside. We say the bone fractured. The doctor might tell you, "You've fractured your wrist."

Notice: your wrist is still there, still in one piece visually. It wasn't snapped in two. But the internal structure of the bone now has a crack — and that crack is serious because it damages the bone's ability to hold weight and function correctly. That internal structural damage is the essence of what "fracture" captures.

Similarly:

  • An earthquake can fracture rock layers underground — cracking the solid rock through immense pressure.
  • Extreme cold can fracture a pipe — the pressure of freezing water cracks the rigid metal from within.
  • A heavy impact can fracture a tile on the floor — you might see a crack running across it, but the tile is still sitting in place.

In all of these cases, the common thread is: something hard and solid develops a crack or break in its structure due to force or pressure.
The Spectrum: From Hairline to Complete

One reason "fracture" is such a useful word is that it covers a range of severity.

On the less severe end, there is something called a hairline fracture — a crack so thin it is almost like a hair drawn across the surface of the bone. It is barely visible, but it is there, and it is painful. On the more severe end, the bone could fracture so badly that it breaks into multiple pieces. Both situations use the word "fracture" because they share the same process: the structural integrity of something hard was broken.

This means "fracture" can describe mild structural damage or severe damage, but it always implies that the damage is real and meaningful — not just a surface scratch.

Here is where the word becomes even more powerful. "Fracture" is also used to describe the breaking apart of things that are not physical — things like relationships, communities, trust, peace, or unity.

This figurative use works because of the logic of the physical meaning: just as a bone fractures when something that was strong and solid gets damaged under pressure, an abstract "solid" thing — like a friendship, a team, or a nation — can fracture when the pressures on it become too great.

For example:

  • "Years of disagreement finally fractured the political party." — The party was once unified and strong. Now it has cracked internally, with groups pulling in different directions.
  • "The betrayal fractured their friendship." — What was once a solid, reliable bond now has a deep crack running through it.
  • "The scandal fractured public trust in the institution." — The trust people had was like a firm foundation. The scandal cracked it.

Notice the pattern: in figurative use, "fracture" is chosen when what breaks was previously strong, unified, and stable. The word carries a sense of seriousness — this is not a small falling-out. Something that was structurally sound has been meaningfully damaged.

The verb "fracture" can be used in two ways grammatically:

1. Something causes something else to fracture (transitive):
Here, there is a clear actor doing the fracturing.

  • "The impact fractured his collarbone."
  • "The disagreement fractured the alliance."

2. Something fractures on its own (intransitive):
Here, the focus is on what happened to the thing itself, not on what caused it.

  • "His leg fractured under the weight."
  • "The coalition fractured after the election."

Both uses are completely correct and common.

"Break" is a broad, general word. You can break a promise, break a record, break water, or break the silence. It covers an enormous range of situations.

"Fracture," by contrast, is precise and focused. It is chosen specifically when:

  • The thing being damaged is hard and rigid (physically), or strong and unified (figuratively).
  • The damage involves a crack or split in the structure, not just surface-level damage.
  • The thing does not necessarily fall apart completely — it may still hold together but be internally compromised.

A glass can break in many ways, but if you say it fractured, you are painting a specific picture: a crack or split running through the hard material, damaging it structurally. If you said it shattered, you'd be picturing it exploding into many pieces. "Fracture" sits between an ordinary crack and total destruction — it is serious structural damage.

To fracture something is to crack or break its internal structure under force, in a way that damages its ability to hold together and function properly. The key ideas to hold onto are:

  • It applies to things that are hard and solid (physically) or strong and stable (figuratively).
  • It does not always mean complete separation into pieces — a fracture is often an internal crack.
  • It describes serious, structural damage — more than a scratch, sometimes less than total destruction.
  • It can be used for bones, rock, glass, and ice, but equally powerfully for relationships, communities, trust, and unity.

When you see or hear the word "fracture" used as a verb, your mind should immediately picture something that was once whole and strong — now cracked from within.
6549:
Fragile describes something that breaks, cracks, or gets damaged very easily. If something is fragile, it cannot handle rough handling, pressure, or stress — even a small amount of force or disturbance is enough to damage or destroy it. Think of a thin wine glass. You don't need to throw it against a wall to break it. Just dropping it from a short height, or knocking it gently off a table, is enough. That glass is fragile.

The most important thing to understand is this: fragile describes a built-in weakness — a quality the thing has before anything goes wrong. It doesn't mean the thing is already broken. It means it could break very easily.

In its most straightforward use, fragile describes physical objects that are easily broken or damaged. Old pottery, thin glass, dry autumn leaves, a bird's egg — these are all fragile. They require careful handling. This is why you often see the word "FRAGILE" printed on boxes containing things like electronics or glassware. It is a warning: handle this with care, because it will not take much to damage it.

Here is where the word becomes truly powerful. Fragile is not just about physical objects. It is used very widely to describe anything — a situation, a person, a system, an emotion — that can fall apart or be harmed easily. This is the figurative use of the word, and you will encounter it constantly.

A fragile person is someone whose physical health is poor and can get worse very easily. An elderly patient recovering from surgery, for example, may be described as fragile. It signals that they need to be treated with great care, because their body cannot take much strain.

A fragile situation is one that is unstable and could go wrong very quickly. Imagine two countries that recently stopped fighting a war. The peace between them is fragile — one wrong move, one provocation, and the peace could collapse entirely.

A fragile economy is one that appears to be functioning, but is built on shaky foundations. A small crisis — a stock market drop, a natural disaster, a political shock — could cause it to crumble.

A fragile relationship is one where trust, connection, or goodwill is thin. It has not been built on a strong foundation, so a disagreement or betrayal could end it easily.

An emotionally fragile person is someone who is psychologically vulnerable at a particular moment. They are easily hurt by criticism, bad news, or conflict. This does not mean they are a weak person in character — it often means they are going through a very hard time and their emotional reserves are low.

A fragile ego describes someone who cannot handle criticism or challenges to their self-image. The smallest negative comment feels like a devastating attack to them, because their sense of self-worth is not firmly grounded.

In all of these uses, the same core idea holds: something that looks like it's holding together, but won't take much to break it.
The Key Distinction: Fragile vs. Already Broken

This is important. Something fragile is at risk of breaking — it has not necessarily broken yet. A fragile ceasefire is still a ceasefire. A fragile ecosystem is still functioning. The word signals danger and the need for care, not failure that has already happened.
How Fragile Compares to Similar Words

Delicate is the closest word to fragile, and they are often interchangeable. However, delicate often carries a sense of beauty, refinement, or intricacy alongside the sense of being easily damaged. A spider's web is delicate — it is both fragile and intricate. Fragile, on the other hand, focuses purely on the tendency to break or fail, with no implication of beauty.

Brittle is more specific. A brittle material snaps suddenly and completely when force is applied — it does not bend or stretch first. It's a more technical or physical word. Fragile is broader and more commonly used.

Weak means lacking strength, but it does not always imply easy breakage. A weak argument is not a convincing one, but you would not call it fragile. Fragile specifically suggests the risk of coming apart or being damaged.

Vulnerable describes exposure to danger or harm, but it does not necessarily mean something will break easily. A child alone in a dangerous city is vulnerable, but you would not call them fragile (unless their health was also poor). Fragile focuses on the structural weakness of a thing, while vulnerable focuses more on its exposure to risk.

To understand a word fully, it helps to know what it stands against. The opposites of fragile are words like sturdy, robust, durable, resilient, and strong. A robust system can absorb shocks and still function. A resilient person can face hardship and recover. These words describe the kind of strength and stability that fragile things lack.

• The noun is fragility — the quality of being fragile. ("The fragility of the old manuscript made it difficult to handle.")
  • The adverb is fragilely, though this is rarely used in everyday speech.

Fragile means easily broken, damaged, or destroyed — whether you are talking about a glass object, a person's health, a political situation, a relationship, or someone's emotions. It always signals that something requires care, because it lacks the strength to withstand pressure or disruption. The fragility exists before the breaking — it is a warning, not a verdict.
